column3: X · THREADS · BLUESKY — where people say it in one breath and argue under it. Read your list through `batch`, each post whole, and give every printed row its verdict: a sentence that carries a verdict, a switch or a complaint goes in with `add`, a row that says nothing gets `verdict none`. When a post's replies matter, `fetch` its address — the post AND its replies (`opencli twitter thread` stands behind it for X) — and batch prints it again, whole. When batch has nothing left, search your platforms yourself with every tool you carry (`opencli twitter search`, `opencli bluesky thread`, `hidden.py read` for a Threads post) and `fetch` and `add` what you find. Your line says who said it, when, and how many replies agreed.

THE SPOKEN WORD — YouTube · TikTok · Instagram · Bilibili: the videos where people TEST the subject. `batch` hands you what was actually SAID in each video (the transcript) and the comments under it; `add` the sentences that narrate what happened over real use and give every other printed row `verdict none`. TikTok and Instagram captions and comments come the same way. When batch has nothing left, search further with every tool you carry (`opencli tiktok search` finds more) and `fetch` and `add` what you find. Bilibili addresses are rows of the `chinese` platform, which is the foreign hunter's list — search Bilibili yourself (`opencli bilibili search`) and add a decisive one the same way.

THE CROWD — the forums where ordinary users argue: Reddit · Hacker News · lobste.rs · Stack Overflow · Quora. Read EVERY thread on your list through `batch` (the thread in full, comments included), `add` the voices and give every printed row its verdict; search further with every tool you carry and `fetch` and `add` what you find; then run crowd.sh over ALL the thread addresses (not the first three) and count the people inside — that number is the denominator of the whole fleet, and the fleet counts it once more itself after you. How many separate humans said something, and what each side's share is.

THE PROFESSIONALS — LinkedIn · Facebook · Substack · Medium: where people write under their own name and job. Read your list through `batch` and give every printed row its verdict; when batch has nothing left, find more LinkedIn posts with `mcpx.sh exa "linkedin.com/posts <q>" 10`, Facebook groups and posts with `opencli facebook search`, Substack and Medium with their own `search`, and `fetch` (the hidden signed-in browser stands behind it) and `add` what you find. `add` the first-hand sentences — a vendor's own announcement is not evidence here.

THE CODE AND THE NUMBERS — GitHub · npm/PyPI · leaderboards · papers: what actually breaks in the open, and what independent measurement says. Read every GitHub issue, pull request and README on your list through `batch` and give every printed row its verdict; search further with 4-word token queries (`gh search issues`), not sentences. For numbers, open the leaderboards, benchmark pages, package pages and papers (arxiv · crossref · openalex · europepmc) with `fetch`, which reads JavaScript pages through the hidden browser. Every number goes in with `add`, with its date and who produced it.

THE OTHER LANGUAGES — zhihu · v2ex · linux.do · weibo · juejin · xiaohongshu · bilibili, and the German and Turkish forums. The non-English crowd often tests things nobody in English has written about yet. `add` the ORIGINAL sentence: a translation is not in the body and is refused; the session translates when it writes the answer.

THE COUNTER-CASE, ON EVERY PLATFORM — you hunt the OPPOSITE of whatever the obvious answer is: "why we moved off X", "switched back to Y", "X is overrated", "X production problems", "regret", "cancelled my subscription". Your list is every platform no other hunter of this run owns — the open web above all: blogs, news, comparisons, lobste.rs. Bring the strongest case for the other side, with names and dates, and say plainly if it is weak — that is also a finding.
